source.title_on_document: Training novices to think, or giving them LLMs? Evidence from an RCT

supplement.where: Appendix Sections 1-6, PDF pp. 17-49 [printed pp. 16-48]. The main text explicitly refers to these materials (PDF p. 3). No separate external supplement is identified. The AEA registration link and number are withheld (PDF pp. 3, 17).
supplement.holds: Experimental procedures, scoring rubrics, evaluator training, reliability (Table A.3), idea extraction and embedding methods, full-sample descriptive statistics (Table A.7), arm counts and balance checks (Table A.8), and coefficient tables with SEs (Tables A.9-A.14). These tables do not report arm-level outcome SDs; Table A.7 reports full-sample SDs.

paper_design_summary: A factorial classroom RCT randomized 13 classes to causal-reasoning training or a placebo game, crossed with ChatGPT Edu access or no access. The main analyses include 1,053 first-year students who wrote merchandising recommendations during regular course time; 1,051 were analyzed where within-solution diversity was required. Recommendations were scored for marketing effectiveness, expert alignment, idea count, semantic diversity within and between participants, and causal reasoning (PDF pp. 17-19, 23-24, 29, 41-48).

studies.label: Classroom factorial RCT: causal-reasoning training and ChatGPT Edu access

assignment.what_was_assigned: Intact classes were randomized within bachelor program to Control (placebo, no AI), Causal (training, no AI), GPT (placebo, AI), or Causal&GPT (training, AI). One class per program entered each arm, except that two Management-program classes entered Causal&GPT. The study reports a between-subjects design conducted in November 2025 (PDF p. 17).
assignment.quote: The treatments of our research design are randomized at the class level: we assign one intact class per program to each of the four arms.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 17 [printed p. 16], Appendix Section 1; PDF p. 2 [printed p. 1], Introduction.
assignment.prereg_locator: PDF p. 17 [printed p. 16], Appendix Section 1, states registration with the AEA RCT Registry before data collection. PDF p. 3 [printed p. 2], footnote 2, withholds the registration number. The preregistration itself is not available in the supplied material.

arms.name: Control
arms.description: Placebo game (same 12 questions, no scaffolding or feedback), no ChatGPT during the case

arms.name: Causal
arms.description: Causal-reasoning training game (12 binary-choice questions with worked examples and feedback), reminder prompt before the case, no ChatGPT

arms.name: GPT
arms.description: Placebo game, then ChatGPT Edu (GPT-4o) available in a separate browser tab during the case

arms.name: Causal&GPT
arms.description: Causal-reasoning training game plus reminder prompt, then ChatGPT Edu (GPT-4o) available during the case

participants.exclusions: No participant exclusions or attrition flow are reported. The abstract says 1,053 students were assigned; the Introduction reports the four assigned conditions with 249/256/197/351 participants, also shown in Table A.8 (PDF pp. 1-2, 43). These are participating students in the unannounced class sessions, not an independently reported count of everyone enrolled in the randomized classes (PDF p. 3). Main outcome analyses use 1,053 students except within-solution diversity, which uses 1,051 because two responses have only one core idea (PDF p. 42; Table A.12, PDF p. 46). PDS models incorporating that diversity measure also use 1,051 (Table A.13 cols. 2-3, PDF p. 47; Table A.14 cols. 2-3, 5-6, 8-9, PDF p. 48). Self-declared GPT compliance is 90.5% overall, 88% in GPT and 92% in Causal&GPT (PDF p. 2, footnote 1); no exclusion for noncompliance is reported.
participants.who: First-year undergraduates in 13 class sections of an introductory Management course across economics and management, economics and finance, and management bachelor programs (PDF p. 17).
participants.quote: we assign 1,053 first-year undergraduates in economics, management and finance to one of four conditions
participants.locator: PDF p. 1, Abstract (assigned students); PDF p. 17, Appendix Section 1 (sample and classes); PDF p. 23, Appendix Section 2.4 (responses scored); PDF pp. 42-48, Tables A.7-A.14 (analysis counts). Country is not explicitly stated; Appendix references Bocconi registrar records (PDF p. 36), and the case names Bocconi and Milan (PDF pp. 30-31).

ai_tool.how_used: AI-arm students could use ChatGPT Edu while writing the recommendation, through an institutional subscription in a separate browser tab; non-AI arms did not have this access. The post-survey invited AI-arm students to share conversation logs. GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and embedding models used later for measurement were not the assigned assistance tool. PDF p. 7, Section 4.2; PDF p. 18, Appendix Section 1.

task.description: Write a consultant-style recommendation to increase alumni awareness and usage of university-branded merchandise, using supplied information about sales channels, prices, and the 144,000+ alumni base. The main text asks for up to 180 words; the Appendix and reproduced task ask for approximately 180 words (PDF pp. 7, 18, 31).
task.duration: The main text calls this a 45-minute case (PDF pp. 3, 7), whereas the Appendix says the entire session lasted approximately 45 minutes, with early completion or a few extra minutes allowed (PDF p. 17). A consistent separate case-only duration cannot be confirmed.

outcomes.name: Awareness and usage evaluation score
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Twenty trained master's students, predominantly in management and marketing, described as human experts with work experience (PDF pp. 7-8, Section 4.2), blinded to condition and hypotheses (PDF p. 22, Appendix Section 2.3). Each recommendation received three ratings, for 3,159 ratings total. Each rater averaged two 1-5 scores (awareness and usage), then the three rater scores were averaged at participant level (PDF p. 23, Section 2.4). Table A.3 reports ICC 0.544 overall; Control 0.275, Causal 0.322, GPT 0.534, Causal X GPT 0.493. The construct is effectiveness of the proposed marketing strategies, coded usefulness, not a direct originality rating (PDF p. 18). PDS robustness/mediation models add reasoning/idea, diversity, and text controls: GPT coefficients 0.490*** (SE 0.045), 0.448*** (0.053), 0.362*** (0.056), N=1,053/1,051/1,051 (Table A.13, PDF pp. 46-47).

contrasts.reported: Table A.10 OLS, clustered SEs in parentheses. No balance controls: GPT 0.834*** (0.100), Causal -0.101 (0.068), Causal x GPT 0.072 (0.125), constant 2.236*** (0.040). With balance controls: GPT 0.862*** (0.079), Causal -0.111*** (0.040), Causal x GPT 0.082 (0.084), constant 2.089*** (0.230). N=1053 in each model. Constants are regression intercepts, not reported adjusted arm means. Full-sample outcome mean 2.635, SD 0.843 (Table A.7). *** p<0.01. The GPT coefficient compares GPT with Control; the interaction is not the Causal&GPT-versus-Causal effect.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 45 [printed p. 44], Table A.10 cols. 1-2 and note; PDF p. 42 [printed p. 41], Table A.7; PDF p. 8, Section 4.2.

outcomes.name: Number of ideas in the solution (core ideas)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of distinct core ideas extracted using GPT-5.2: three prompt variants with five repeated runs each plus the original run; an idea is confirmed in at least two of sixteen runs. Uncertain matches use GPT-5.2 and Claude Opus 4.6 judges. Italian responses are translated to English during extraction (PDF p. 41, Appendix Section 4). Full-sample mean 6.756, SD 3.170, N=1053 (Table A.7, PDF p. 42). Figure 5 shows SD-normalized coefficients; no numerical values are read off the graph.

outcomes.name: Within-solution diversity of ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Mean pairwise cosine distance among the core ideas within one participant's response, using text-embedding-3-large. Two responses with one core idea have undefined distances and are missing. This is flexibility (variety within one person), rather than diversity across people. N=1051, full-sample mean 0.596, SD 0.078 (PDF pp. 41-42, Appendix Section 4 and Table A.7). Figure 5 displays SD-normalized coefficients.

contrasts.reported: OLS with balance controls; standard errors clustered by mother tongue x high-school type x degree class. Table A.12 col. 2: GPT 0.009** (SE 0.005), Causal 0.043*** (0.006), Causal x GPT -0.001 (0.008), constant 0.541*** (0.025); N=1051; 50 clusters. ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01, copied as printed despite rounded coefficients and SEs. The text says GPT has a positive but much smaller effect than Causal. No inference for the Causal&GPT-versus-Causal coefficient sum is supplied by the near-zero interaction alone.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 46 [printed p. 45], Table A.12 col. 2 and note; PDF p. 11 [printed p. 10], Figure 5 and Section 4.3; PDF p. 42, Appendix Section 4 (missing values).

outcomes.name: Between-solution diversity of ideas
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Mean cosine distance of a participant's core ideas from all other students' ideas in the pooled sample, calculated with text-embedding-3-large. Higher values mean greater difference from the full response pool; the reference pool is not restricted to the participant's treatment arm. Full-sample mean 0.624, SD 0.038, N=1053 (PDF pp. 41-42, Appendix Section 4 and Table A.7). Figure 5 displays SD-normalized coefficients.

diversity_detail.metric: Mean cosine distance of a participant's extracted core ideas from other participants' ideas; higher is more diverse.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: OpenAI text-embedding-3-large; Italian responses translated into English during GPT-5.2 idea extraction (PDF p. 41).
diversity_detail.computed_over: Other participants in the full pooled sample across all four arms. The Appendix says "N = 1,052 comparisons per idea" (PDF p. 42); Table A.12 says all other responses in the sample (1,052). One dependent-variable score per participant. The precise weighting across multiple ideas in other responses is not specified.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: OLS of participant scores with balance controls; SEs clustered by mother tongue x high-school type x degree class (50 clusters), as printed in Table A.12, PDF p. 46. These subdivide the 13 assigned classes rather than clustering at the assignment unit (class definition and clustering construction, PDF p. 37).
diversity_detail.notes: No sign reversal is needed for this distance measure. It measures distance from the pooled response distribution, not within-arm homogeneity. Within-arm similarity and randomization-class clustered precision are not reported.

outcomes.name: Similarity of participant solution to expert solutions (Mkt Professor, Merchandising expert, Expert Alumnus)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Three reference-specific measures of the same expert-alignment outcome: one minus cosine distance between each recommendation and a marketing professor, merchandising manager, or expert alumnus recommendation, using text-embedding-3-large. Comparisons match the participant's survey language; expert texts were translated into Italian (PDF pp. 23-24, Appendix Section 2.4). Full-sample means 0.794/0.753/0.806 and SDs 0.041/0.045/0.050, respectively; N=1053 (Table A.7, PDF p. 42). This is an expert-alignment performance proxy, coded other; it does not measure similarity among experimental participants. PDS robustness/mediation GPT coefficients, with SEs: professor 0.018*** (0.004), 0.014*** (0.003), 0.008** (0.004); merchandising expert 0.016*** (0.004), 0.011*** (0.003), 0.008** (0.003); alumnus 0.030*** (0.004), 0.025*** (0.003), 0.016*** (0.003). N=1,053/1,051/1,051 in each set. *** p<0.01, ** p<0.05 (Table A.14, PDF p. 48).

contrasts.reported: Table A.11 OLS; clustered SEs; N=1053 throughout. GPT coefficients without/with balance controls: Marketing professor 0.028*** (SE 0.007) / 0.026*** (0.004); merchandising expert 0.030*** (0.007) / 0.028*** (0.005); expert alumnus 0.044*** (0.006) / 0.044*** (0.005). Corresponding interactions: 0.003 (0.010) / 0.003 (0.004); -0.007 (0.009) / -0.007 (0.006); -0.002 (0.007) / -0.002 (0.006). Causal and interaction coefficients have no significance stars in any column. *** p<0.01. Positive direction means closer to expert reference answers, not greater novelty.

eligibility.reason: All three criteria are met in S1. Intact classes were randomized within bachelor program to ChatGPT Edu (GPT-4o) access or no access, crossed with causal-reasoning training; AI was available while recommendations were written (PDF pp. 2, 17-18). The main analyses include 1,053 people; 1,051 were analyzed for within-solution diversity and models requiring that measure because two responses contained only one core idea (PDF p. 42; Tables A.9-A.14, PDF pp. 44-48). Participants produced open-ended merchandising recommendations, scored for effectiveness, idea count, within-person flexibility, and diversity across participants (PDF pp. 18-19, 23, 41-42). The diversity measure directly compares different participants' outputs and satisfies criterion 3 even though its reference pool combines all arms. Regular course sessions support field_rct. Missing direct combined-arm contrast estimates, arm-level SDs, within-arm diversity, and assignment-class clustered SEs constrain later extraction or pooling, not these eligibility criteria. Reported SEs use 50 clustering cells rather than the 13 randomized classes (PDF pp. 17, 37, 46-48).

one_line_finding: ChatGPT increased recommendation usefulness by 0.862 points (SE 0.079) and idea count by 2.251 (SE 0.290), with no clear effect on between-person diversity (-0.002, SE 0.002); causal training increased diversity by 0.018 (SE 0.003) (Tables A.10 and A.12, PDF pp. 45-46).
open_questions: Country is not explicitly stated. The Appendix names Bocconi registrar records and the case names Milan, but country is left null under the source-only rule.

The separate Causal&GPT-versus-Causal estimates and their SEs/tests are not printed. For usefulness, idea count, and expert alignment, a direct contrast direction is left null rather than inferred from component coefficients.
The AEA registry identifier/link is withheld. The paper calls the human evaluation its main result; primary/secondary priority for the other outcomes cannot be verified and is coded not_stated.

Randomization-class clustered SEs are not reported; current precision uses cells defined by class, mother tongue, and high-school type. Suitable class-level precision would be needed for pooling under codebook Section 10.
Arm-level outcome SDs and within-arm semantic diversity are not reported. The precise averaging weights in the pooled between-person distance measure are not specified.
Case-only duration is inconsistent between main text and Appendix; both descriptions are retained.
notes: Read all 1,796 lines of the markdown, including all Appendix sections and references, and checked recorded numbers against PDF text. Outcome IDs follow A for the five shared outcomes, with the three B-only reasoning outcomes retained as S1-O6 to S1-O8; differing order/IDs in B are not substantive disagreements. GPT versus Control is the direct printed AI comparison without causal training. The factorial GPT and interaction coefficients are distinct from Causal&GPT versus Causal; no coefficients were summed and no effect sizes were computed. All outcome availability codes refer to the AI arms while writing, not to AI measurement conducted afterward. No after_ai output was assessed. Games were completed before AI access; self-reported attitudes and text features used only as controls are not separate outcomes. Source Table A.7 reports CRT mean 0.490 whereas Table A.8 reports 0.769 (PDF pp. 42-43); this unrelated baseline inconsistency is not used in eligibility or outcome extraction. Blinding and rater reliability describe measurement, not additional independent participants. The adjusted Table A.10 constant is an intercept and is not labeled an observed control mean. No external API or web source was used. Finalization: all three challenge files (assignment, outcome, people) contain empty problems arrays, so challenge_resolution is empty and all challenge-action counts are zero. The finalizer independently read the complete markdown, including the Appendix, and checked eligibility passages, recorded participant counts, scoring methods, and outcome statistics against PDF text. The included supplement and field_rct coding already match the current spec. All six open questions and all four unresolved reconciliation differences are covered in final.open_items; none affects eligibility. posted_data identifies material that would settle an item, not an assertion that a data repository is currently available. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged.

differences.a: ChatGPT access raised the rater-scored awareness-and-usage score by 0.862 points on a 1-5 scale (SE 0.079; control constant 2.089) and the number of core ideas by 2.251 (SE 0.290), but left between-participant idea diversity unchanged (-0.002, SE 0.002) (Tables A.10 and A.12, pp. 44-45).
differences.b: ChatGPT access raised rater scores of the recommendations (GPT 0.862, SE 0.079, vs control constant 2.089 on a 1-5 scale) and the number of ideas (2.251, SE 0.290) but did not change between-participant idea diversity (-0.002, SE 0.002), while causal training raised it (0.018, SE 0.003) (Tables A.10 and A.12, PDF pp. 45-46).
differences.resolved: ChatGPT increased recommendation usefulness by 0.862 points (SE 0.079) and idea count by 2.251 (SE 0.290), with no clear effect on between-person diversity (-0.002, SE 0.002); causal training increased diversity by 0.018 (SE 0.003) (Tables A.10 and A.12, PDF pp. 45-46).

open_items.item: Country of the participant sample is not explicitly stated; keep participants.country null. Author confirmation of the trial location would settle open_questions[0] and the unresolved reconciliation difference studies.S1.participants.country. The main text withholds the institution, while the Appendix names Bocconi registrar records and the case names Milan (PDF pp. 3, 30-31, 36); country is not an eligibility requirement.

The Causal&GPT-versus-Causal usefulness estimate, SE, and test are not printed separately (Table A.10, PDF p. 45). Participant-level data with assignment and model covariates, or the fitted model covariance, would permit that contrast. This covers the usefulness part of open_questions[1] and unresolved studies.S1.outcomes.S1-O1.contrasts.Causal&GPT_vs_Causal; the printed GPT-versus-Control contrast already supports an eligible comparison.

The Causal&GPT-versus-Causal idea-count estimate, SE, and test are not printed separately (Table A.12 column 1, PDF p. 46). Participant-level data with assignment and model covariates, or the fitted model covariance, would permit that contrast. This covers the idea-count part of open_questions[1] and unresolved studies.S1.outcomes.S1-O2.contrasts.Causal&GPT_vs_Causal; it does not change the randomized design, sample size, or output scoring.

The Causal&GPT-versus-Causal expert-alignment estimates, SEs, and tests are not printed separately for any expert reference (Table A.11, PDF p. 45). Participant-level data with assignment and model covariates, or the fitted model covariances, would permit those contrasts. This covers the expert-alignment part of open_questions[1] and unresolved studies.S1.outcomes.S1-O5.contrasts.Causal&GPT_vs_Causal; the other eligible output measures remain available.

The AEA registry identifier/link and preregistered outcome priority remain unavailable (open_questions[2]; PDF pp. 3, 17). Authors would need to supply the registry entry or original analysis plan to verify priority beyond the human evaluation identified as the main result (PDF p. 7). Preregistration and outcome priority are not required for these eligibility criteria.

Assignment-class clustered precision is not reported (open_questions[3]). The paper randomizes 13 classes but reports SEs clustered by mother tongue, high-school type, and class, with 50 cells (PDF pp. 17, 37, 46-48). Participant-level outcomes, assignment, class identifiers, and model covariates would support re-estimation at the randomized class level. This affects suitability for pooling under codebook Section 10, not screening eligibility.

Arm-level outcome SDs are not reported; Table A.7 provides only full-sample outcome SDs (open_questions[4]; PDF p. 42). Participant-level outcomes and arm membership would settle the missing arm-level summaries. This concerns effect-size extraction and standardization, not eligibility.

Within-arm between-person semantic diversity is not reported (open_questions[4]). The recorded measure compares each participant with the full pooled sample (PDF p. 42; Table A.12 note, PDF p. 46). Participant texts or extracted ideas/embeddings, arm membership, and analysis code would permit a within-arm calculation. The existing pooled-reference measure already scores diversity across participants and satisfies criterion 3.

The exact averaging weights across ideas and other responses in the pooled between-person distance measure are unspecified (open_questions[4]; PDF pp. 41-42, 46). An explicit formula or implementation from the authors would settle the weighting. This affects reproducibility and interpretation; the source already establishes that different participants' outputs are compared.

Case-only duration remains inconsistent (open_questions[5]): the main text describes a 45-minute case, whereas the Appendix gives approximately 45 minutes for the full session (PDF pp. 3, 7, 17). Authors would need to clarify the task-specific time allowance or session protocol. Both descriptions are retained; the discrepancy does not affect randomization, the analyzed sample size, or output scoring.
